title: How Orchids Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant cover orchids: their growth habits (monopodial vs. sympodial), habitats (terrestrial, epiphytes, lithophytes), the Victorian-era orchid mania and orchid hunters, pollination tricks (sexual deception by bee-mimicking flowers, hornet-luring flowers, rotting-flesh pollinators), Darwin's prediction of the long-tongued Madagascar moth, vanilla as an orchid, and home orchid care (repotting, watering, fertilizing, humidity). The episode also includes casual banter about holiday food, dogs, and the film Adaptation, plus a listener mail segment responding to criticism of the show's broad overviews and a flight attendant's response about pay and training.

segments.title: Opening banter and holiday party talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with chatter about the Christmas season, holiday party food, and the fact that this is the last recording of the year. They introduce the orchid topic and Chuck's new interest in growing orchids.

segments.title: Caring for orchids after blooming
segments.summary: Josh explains how to keep an orchid after it stops flowering: repot it, replace sphagnum moss with wood chips or orchid mix, and water and fertilize weekly so it can rebloom.

segments.title: Orchid mania and orchid hunters
segments.summary: The hosts describe the number of orchid species and hybrids and the Victorian-era orchid craze in England, when orchid hunters collected plants from Central and South America for wealthy collectors. Frederick Sander is named as the royal orchid grower for Queen Victoria.

segments.title: Orchids' popularity and sexual imagery
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how orchids became cheap and widespread, citing Michael Pollan's essay. They talk about why humans find orchids attractive, including bilateral symmetry and suggestive shapes, and the Victorian opposition to the craze. The name orchid comes from a Greek word for testicle, referring to the bulb.

segments.title: Orchid growth habits and where they live
segments.summary: The hosts explain monopodial and sympodial growth habits, and terrestrial, epiphytic, and lithophytic orchids. They note epiphytes and lithophytes are not parasitic, taking nutrients from decomposing debris rather than from their host.

segments.title: Orchid seeds, fungi, and pollination tricks
segments.summary: Orchid seeds are dust seeds that need a symbiotic fungus to germinate, so growing from seed is slow and rare. Orchids produce pollinia and rely on tricks such as mimicking female bees to attract male bees, and luring hornets with bee-fear pheromones. Michael Pollan's essay is cited on how slight variations keep bees from learning to avoid the flowers. One orchid mimics the smell of rotting flesh to attract flies and carrion beetles.

segments.title: Darwin's moth prediction and vanilla
segments.summary: The hosts describe Darwin's 1862 prediction of a long-tongued moth for a Madagascar orchid with a long nectary, which was confirmed decades later with the discovery of a moth and filmed feeding about a hundred years later. They then note vanilla is an orchid, and the flavor comes from the seeds inside the bean.

segments.title: Orchid care: light, humidity, water, and potting media
segments.summary: The hosts discuss care needs: leaf texture as a light clue, indirect light, high humidity and warm temperatures for tropical orchids, daylight hours, avoiding overwatering, using pine bark or moss, and using dilute liquid orchid fertilizer. Josh describes his routine. Chuck recounts repotting a rotting orchid and dusting roots with cinnamon.

segments.title: Closing and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the orchid discussion and mention the Orchid Thief and Adaptation before transitioning to listener mail. Josh reads a flight attendant's response about pay for delays and training scores, and the closing credits list contact information.
